notice verb

see, become aware of

also notice that, spot, take notice

classical

Aug. Conf. 6.6.9: animadvertī pauperem mendīcum
Cic. Off. 1.145
Traupman 352

animadvertō, animadvertere, animadvertī, animadversum

verb, third conjugation

notice, observe

From animum advertere, “turn the mind to”, which Cato and Cicero still write as two words (Agr. 1.2; Tusc. 5.65). With an accusative, an accusative and infinitive (notice that …) or a question (Lewis & Short). What one notices by ear or by touch is often sentīre (see feel).

Examples

  • animadvertī pauperem mendīcum, jam, crēdō, saturum, jocantem atque laetantem

    I noticed a poor beggar, already full, I suppose, joking and cheerfulAug. Conf. 6.6.9

  • ut in fidibus aut tībiīs, quamvīs paulum discrepent, tamen id ā sciente animadvertī solet

    as with strings or pipes: however slightly they are out of tune, an expert still notices itCic. Off. 1.145

  • ego autem cum omnia conlūstrārem oculīs … animum advertī columellam nōn multum ē dūmīs ēminentem

    as I was looking all around … I noticed a little column standing a short way out of the bramblesCic. Tusc. 5.65

Other words

  • cōnspiciō, cōnspicere, cōnspexī, cōnspectum — catch sight of, spot

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Phaedr. 1.24.2: rāna cōnspexit bovem

See also feel, sign, pay attention!, recognize.

SourcesLewis & Short: animadverto · Lewis & Short: conspicio
